---
title: "Block Kriging and the Difference Estimator"
subtitle: "From point predictions to an exact domain mean, and from the map to a design-based correction"
bibliography: ../paper/references.bib
---

## Summary

The target is a domain mean $\theta_y=\int Z\,d\mathbb P_y$. The estimator has two parts: a map $\hat Z=\hat\mu+\hat a$ (mean
field plus GP-predicted anomaly), and a correction for the map's error built from the floats.

1. **Block kriging is not a new predictor.** It is the *exact integral* of the ordinary GP predictive mean. Summing
   point predictions at nodes approximates that integral and adds a quadrature error of the map. No sampling
   correction can remove that error, because it is not a sampling error.
2. **The difference estimator** writes $\theta_y=\int m\,d\mathbb P_y+\int(Z-m)\,d\mathbb P_y$ for any map $m$. The first term is
   computed (by block kriging). The second, the integral of the map's residual, is estimated by inverse-intensity
   weighting of residuals at the profiles (Campbell's theorem). That is the Horvitz--Thompson difference estimator of
   survey sampling, in continuous space-time.
3. **What we add:** cross-fitting over floats, so that residuals come from a map that did not see them; a Hájek
   (calibrated) normalization; and an intensity $\hat q$ estimated by simulation rather than known from a design. The last
   is why the guarantee is *double robustness*, as for AIPW in causal inference, instead of design unbiasedness.

## 1. Setting and estimand

- $x=(s,t)$ is a space-time coordinate: $s$ in the connected $\ge 2000$ m North Atlantic domain $A$, $t$ in days.
  $\mathcal X_y=A\times y$ is the domain-year.
- $\nu$ is area $\times$ time (surface measure on $A$ times Lebesgue measure in days), and
  $\mathbb P_y=\nu(\cdot\cap\mathcal X_y)/\nu(\mathcal X_y)$ is the normalized area-time *probability* measure.
- $Z(x)$ is the true layer OHC (J m$^{-2}$), bounded and measurable on $\mathcal X_y$.

$$
\theta_y=\int_{\mathcal X_y} Z\,d\mathbb P_y \qquad\text{(the area-time mean: the estimand).}
$$

Profiles form a point process $N$ on $\mathcal X_y$ with intensity measure $\Lambda(E)=\mathbb E\,N(E)$. We assume
$\Lambda\ll\nu$ and write its density as $q=d\Lambda/d\nu$ (expected profiles per km$^2$ per day). We observe $Z(x_i)$ at the
points $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of $N$.

::: {.callout-note}
## Intuition
$\theta_y$ is a fixed number, the mean of one ocean. The randomness is *where the floats went*. Every statement
about bias below is an expectation over $N$ with $Z$ held fixed. That is the design-based view.
:::

## 2. Point kriging (GP regression of the anomaly)

**Working model.** The standard decomposition for mapping OHC [@kuusela2018] is

$$
Z(x)=\mu(x)+a(x)+\varepsilon(x),
$$

where $\mu$ is the climatological mean field (seasonal harmonics and a trend, fitted by local polynomial regression),
$a$ is a zero-mean anomaly field with covariance kernel $k(x,x')$, and $\varepsilon$ is a zero-mean nugget, uncorrelated in
space and time, with variance $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$. Given a fitted mean $\hat\mu$, the residual field and its observations are

$$
r(x):=Z(x)-\hat\mu(x)\approx a(x)+\varepsilon(x),\qquad \mathbf r=\big(r(x_1),\dots,r(x_n)\big)^\top .
$$

Our kernel is the anisotropic exponential $k(x,x')=\sigma_a^2\exp\{-\lVert D^{-1}(x-x')\rVert\}$, with
$D=\operatorname{diag}(\ell_{\mathrm{lon}},\ell_{\mathrm{lat}},\ell_t)$ and hyperparameters $(\sigma_a^2,D,\sigma_\varepsilon^2)$ fitted per region
(locally stationary).

**Notation** [@rasmussen2006, Sec. 2.2]. $K=[k(x_i,x_j)]_{i,j=1}^n$ is the training-training covariance, and for a test point
$x_*$, $\mathbf k_*=[k(x_i,x_*)]_{i=1}^n$ is the training-test covariance. We write the predictive mean as $\hat a$ (their $\bar f_*$) and reserve bars for averages.

**Predictive mean and variance.** Conditioning the Gaussian vector $(a(x_*),\mathbf r)$ gives

$$
\boxed{\;\hat a(x_*)=\mathbf k_*^\top(K+\sigma_\varepsilon^2I)^{-1}\mathbf r,\qquad
\mathbb V[a(x_*)\mid\mathbf r]=k(x_*,x_*)-\mathbf k_*^\top(K+\sigma_\varepsilon^2I)^{-1}\mathbf k_*\;}
$$

and the map is $\hat Z(x_*)=\hat\mu(x_*)+\hat a(x_*)$. Without Gaussianity, $\hat a(x_*)$ is still the best *linear* predictor
(simple kriging): minimizing $\mathbb E\{a(x_*)-\mathbf w^\top\mathbf r\}^2=k(x_*,x_*)-2\mathbf w^\top\mathbf k_*+\mathbf w^\top(K+\sigma_\varepsilon^2I)\mathbf w$
gives $\mathbf w=(K+\sigma_\varepsilon^2I)^{-1}\mathbf k_*$, and the variance above is then its MSE.

Two equivalent readings of the predictive mean:

$$
\hat a(x_*)=\underbrace{\mathbf w^\top\mathbf r}_{\text{weights on the data}}
=\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\,k(x_i,x_*)}_{\text{kernel bumps at the data}},\qquad
\mathbf w=(K+\sigma_\varepsilon^2I)^{-1}\mathbf k_*,\quad
\boldsymbol\alpha=(K+\sigma_\varepsilon^2I)^{-1}\mathbf r .
$$

::: {.callout-note}
## Intuition
**Weights:** $\mathbf w$ is "how correlated each profile is with the target" ($\mathbf k_*$), corrected for "how much the
profiles repeat each other" ($(K+\sigma_\varepsilon^2I)^{-1}$). Ten profiles from one float, close in space and time, count as
little more than one. **Bumps:** the map is a sum of $n$ kernel functions centred on the profiles, with heights
$\alpha_i$ fixed by the data. The test point enters *only* through $k(x_i,x_*)$. That is what makes Section 4 work.
:::

The nugget does not change the predictor. At any $x_*$ off the data, $\operatorname{Cov}\{\varepsilon(x_*),\mathbf r\}=0$, so the best linear
predictor of $Z(x_*)-\hat\mu(x_*)$ is also $\hat a(x_*)$.

In practice each prediction uses only the data in a window around it ($\pm10^\circ$, adjacent months) and the
hyperparameters of its region. This is local GP regression in the sense of @kuusela2018. The model is a *working*
model: it is used to build $\hat Z$, and nothing in Section 5 assumes it is correct.

## 3. From point predictions to the domain mean

Partition $\mathcal X_y$ into blocks $B_j$ (1$^\circ$ cells $\times$ months) with weights $w_j=\mathbb P_y(B_j)$, and put a node
$x_j$ in each block (its area centroid at mid-month). The current map estimate is the quadrature

$$
Q_y(\hat Z)=\sum_j w_j\,\hat Z(x_j).
$$

For any integrable $f$, write $f(B)=\mathbb P_y(B)^{-1}\int_B f\,d\mathbb P_y$ for its block mean. Then, exactly,

$$
Q_y(\hat Z)-\theta_y=\underbrace{\int(\hat Z-Z)\,d\mathbb P_y}_{\text{map error}}
+\underbrace{\sum_j w_j\big[\hat Z(x_j)-\hat Z(B_j)\big]}_{\text{quadrature error of the map}} .
$$

The second term is the gap between the map at the node and the map averaged over its block. A heuristic for its size
(it assumes the map is twice differentiable on the block, which a predictive mean built from exponential kernels is not
at data points): with the node at the block's centroid, the first-order terms cancel and

$$
\hat Z(x_j)-\hat Z(B_j)\approx-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}\!\big(H_j\,S_j\big),
$$

where $H_j$ is the map's Hessian (curvature) and $S_j$ is the block's second-moment matrix about the node. In space,
this is curvature of the mean field over a 1$^\circ$ cell. In time, it is curvature of the seasonal cycle over a month: a
mid-month value is not the monthly mean.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why this term matters
It depends on the node grid, not on the floats. More floats do not shrink it, and correct sampling weights do not
remove it (Section 6).
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Two exact splits, two different remainders
The report on the GLORYS chain splits $Q_y(\hat Z)-\theta_y=[Q_y(\hat Z)-Q_y(Z)]+[Q_y(Z)-\theta_y]$, where the second term is
the quadrature error of the *truth*. Both splits are exact. The one above isolates what block kriging removes: the
quadrature error of the *map*.
:::

## 4. Block kriging

**Target.** Predict the block mean of the anomaly, $a(B)=\mathbb P_y(B)^{-1}\int_B a\,d\mathbb P_y$.

**Derivation.** It is the same conditioning as in Section 2, with $a(x_*)$ replaced by $a(B)$. The only new ingredient
is the covariance between the target and the data. Extend the kernel to blocks by averaging over the test argument;
by Fubini (the kernel is bounded),

$$
k(B,x')=\operatorname{Cov}\big(a(B),a(x')\big)=\frac1{\mathbb P_y(B)}\int_B k(x,x')\,d\mathbb P_y(x),\qquad
k(B,B)=\frac1{\mathbb P_y(B)^2}\iint_{B\times B}k\,d(\mathbb P_y\otimes\mathbb P_y).
$$

With $\mathbf k_B=[k(B,x_i)]_{i=1}^n$ in place of $\mathbf k_*$,

$$
\boxed{\;\hat a(B)=\mathbf k_B^\top(K+\sigma_\varepsilon^2I)^{-1}\mathbf r,\qquad
\mathbb V[a(B)\mid\mathbf r]=k(B,B)-\mathbf k_B^\top(K+\sigma_\varepsilon^2I)^{-1}\mathbf k_B\;}
$$

**The key identity.** In the kernel-bump form, the test point enters only through $k(x_i,\cdot)$, so integrating the map
integrates each bump:

$$
\hat a(B)=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\,k(B,x_i)=\frac1{\mathbb P_y(B)}\int_B\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\,k(x_i,x)\,d\mathbb P_y(x)
=\frac1{\mathbb P_y(B)}\int_B\hat a\,d\mathbb P_y .
$$

**Block kriging is the exact block average of the point predictive mean.** Averaging the kernel first and then solving
gives the same result as predicting every point and then averaging; the first is just the cheap way to compute it.
$K$ and $\boldsymbol\alpha$ are unchanged: only the test vector changes. Adding the block mean of the mean field,
$\hat\mu(B)$, gives

$$
\hat Z(B_j)=\hat\mu(B_j)+\mathbf k_{B_j}^\top(K_j+\sigma_{\varepsilon,j}^2I)^{-1}\mathbf r_j,\qquad
\hat\theta^{\,\mathrm{BK}}_y=\sum_j w_j\,\hat Z(B_j)=\int\tilde Z\,d\mathbb P_y ,
$$

where the subscript $j$ marks block $j$'s window and hyperparameters, and $\tilde Z$ is the map in which every $x\in B_j$
uses them. The quadrature error of the map is gone:

$$
\hat\theta^{\,\mathrm{BK}}_y-\theta_y=\int(\tilde Z-Z)\,d\mathbb P_y \quad\text{exactly.}
$$

**The two terms are integrated separately.** By linearity,

$$
\int\tilde Z\,d\mathbb P_y=\underbrace{\int\tilde\mu\,d\mathbb P_y}_{\text{no kriging}}+\underbrace{\sum_j w_j\,\hat a(B_j)}_{\text{block kriging}} .
$$

Here $\tilde\mu$ is the mean field with block $j$'s local fit on $B_j$. It involves no kernel and no solve. It is a known function, so it is integrated directly over the
domain on as fine a grid as we like, independently of the kriging blocks. Evaluating it at the nodes, $\sum_j w_j\hat\mu(x_j)$,
is the point rule for this term. In the 2020 test it is most of the point rule's error (table below).

::: {.callout-note}
## In practice: only the test vector changes
For each block, both rules use the same window data, the same Cholesky factor of $K_j+\sigma_{\varepsilon,j}^2I$, and the same
$\boldsymbol\alpha_j$. They differ only in where the kernel bumps are read:

| | Point rule | Block rule |
|---|---|---|
| Test vector | $\mathbf k_*=[k(x_j,x_i)]_i$ at the node $x_j$ | $\mathbf k_{B_j}\approx\sum_{x'}\omega_{x'}[k(x',x_i)]_i$ over sub-points $x'\in B_j$ |
| Anomaly | $\mathbf k_*^\top\boldsymbol\alpha_j$ | $\mathbf k_{B_j}^\top\boldsymbol\alpha_j$ |
| Mean field | $\hat\mu(x_j)$ | $\sum_{x'}\omega_{x'}\hat\mu(x')$ |

The $O(n^3)$ factorization is shared. The block rule adds only kernel evaluations at the sub-points.
:::

### What is still numerical

Two integrals of *known, smooth* functions remain.

- $\mathbf k_B$: the kernel averaged over the block. It is computed with sub-points $x'\in B$ and weights $\omega$,
  $k(B,x_i)\approx\sum_{x'}\omega_{x'}k(x',x_i)$ (we use 1/4$^\circ$ cells $\times$ 4 times per month).
- $\int\tilde\mu\,d\mathbb P_y$: the mean field over the domain. Since $\hat\mu(s,t)=\sum_l\gamma_l(s)T_l(t)$ is separable, the time
  integrals of the harmonics and trend over each month have closed forms, and the space integral is a sum over native
  cells. (Planned; the current code averages $\hat\mu$ over the same sub-points as $\mathbf k_B$. A non-separable covariate
  term such as $\log\hat q$ stays on a sub-grid.)

These integrate a smooth, known function, not the eddying field $Z$, so refining the sub-grid drives the error down and
measures it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Preliminary numbers (one replicate, not yet reproduced by repository code)
Replicate 10, 2020, both layers, point rule minus block rule (1/4$^\circ$ $\times$ 4), in GJ m$^{-2}$:

| | 15--700 m | 700--2000 m |
|---|---|---|
| Annual difference, full map | +0.012 | +0.003 |
| ... of which the mean field | +0.012 | +0.004 |
| Months with a positive difference | 11 of 12 | 11 of 12 |

The block estimate converged to about $3\times10^{-5}$ GJ m$^{-2}$ per month (against native cells $\times$ daily), at
6% more compute than the point rule. The point rule's error does not cancel over the year; it is systematic and mostly
in the mean field. The ensemble rerun will replace these numbers.
:::

## 5. The difference estimator

**An exact identity.** For *any* fixed function $m$ on $\mathcal X_y$, with residual $e=Z-m$,

$$
\theta_y=\underbrace{\int m\,d\mathbb P_y}_{\text{computed (block kriging)}}+\underbrace{\int e\,d\mathbb P_y}_{\text{estimated from the floats}} .
$$

We know $m$ everywhere. We know $e$ only at the profiles. (Below, $m$ is a cross-fit map $\tilde Z_{-f}$.)

**Campbell's theorem** [@daley2003]. For any point process with intensity $q$ and measurable $f\ge0$,

$$
\mathbb E\sum_{x\in N}f(x)=\int f\,q\,d\nu .
$$

It needs no independence between points; profiles along one trajectory may be arbitrarily dependent. Taking
$f=e/q$:

$$
\mathbb E\Big[\frac1{\nu(\mathcal X_y)}\sum_{i}\frac{e(x_i)}{q(x_i)}\Big]=\frac1{\nu(\mathcal X_y)}\int e\,d\nu=\int e\,d\mathbb P_y ,
$$

provided $q>0$ $\nu$-a.e. on $\mathcal X_y$ (positivity: every part of the domain can be sampled).

**The HT difference estimator** [@horvitz1952; @sarndal1992]:

$$
\hat\theta^{\,\mathrm{HT}}_y=\int m\,d\mathbb P_y+\frac1{\nu(\mathcal X_y)}\sum_i\frac{e(x_i)}{q(x_i)} .
$$

It is unbiased for **any** map $m$ when $q$ is known.

::: {.callout-note}
## Intuition
Each profile "stands for" $1/q(x_i)$ units of area-time. Where floats crowd, each one stands for little and is
down-weighted. The map does not need to be right for unbiasedness. It needs to be good for *variance*: the correction
averages residuals, so small residuals mean a quiet correction. That is the meaning of *model-assisted, not
model-dependent* [@hansen1983].
:::

### Hájek normalization (what we use)

Replace the known measure $\nu(\mathcal X_y)$ by its own HT estimate, $\nu(\mathcal X_y)\hat\Delta$ with
$\hat\Delta=\nu(\mathcal X_y)^{-1}\sum_i 1/q(x_i)$ (whose expectation is 1). The correction becomes a weighted *mean* of the residuals:

$$
\hat C=\frac{\sum_i v_i\,e(x_i)}{\sum_i v_i},\qquad v_i=\frac1{q(x_i)} .
$$

- **It is calibration.** Rescaling the HT weights so they sum to the known measure gives exactly $\hat C$
  [@deville1992]. It is the simplest case of the g-weighted estimators of model-assisted sampling.
- **The scale of $q$ cancels.** Only the relative intensity matters, which protects against a wrong absolute level
  of $\hat q$ (simulated vs real fleet size).
- **The cost is a ratio bias of order $1/n$.** The exact relation between the two corrections is
  $\hat C_{\mathrm{H}}-\hat C_{\mathrm{HT}}=\hat C_{\mathrm{H}}(1-\hat\Delta)$: the map's mean error times the mass error.
  With a good map the two nearly coincide.

### Cross-fitting over floats

$\hat Z$ is built from the same profiles. A GP predictive mean passes close to its own data, so its residual at a
profile it has seen is artificially small. Summing those residuals misses the very error we want to correct, and
Campbell's theorem no longer applies, because the summand depends on $N$.

The fix is to split the **floats** (not the profiles) into $F$ folds, stratified by launch cohort. For fold $f$, use the map
$\tilde Z_{-f}$ built without fold $f$ (mean field and anomaly both):

$$
\hat\theta^{\,\mathrm{DR}}_y=\frac1F\sum_{f=1}^F\Big\{\int\tilde Z_{-f}\,d\mathbb P_y+\hat C_f\Big\},\qquad
\hat C_f=\frac{\sum_{i\in I_f}v_i\,e_f(x_i)}{\sum_{i\in I_f}v_i},\quad e_f=Z-\tilde Z_{-f}.
$$

- Conditional on everything outside fold $f$ (the $\sigma$-field $\mathcal G_{-f}$), the map is fixed and the fold-$f$ floats are independent draws
  from the deployment law. So Campbell's theorem applies to fold $f$ alone, with fold intensity $q_{f\mid-f}$.
- The folds are units of *floats* because a float's profiles are dependent. Leaving out one profile would leave its
  neighbours on the same trajectory in the map.
- With block kriging, the residual must come from the **same** function that is integrated: $e_f(x_i)$ uses the
  window and hyperparameters of the block containing $x_i$. Then the identity closes exactly.

### An estimated intensity: double robustness

$q$ is not known from a design. It is estimated by simulation, $\hat q$, independently of the data. Write
$\lambda=q/\hat q$ for the intensity error (for fold $f$: $e=e_f$ and $\lambda=q_{f\mid-f}/\hat q_f$, conditional on $\mathcal G_{-f}$).
Campbell's theorem now gives, for the HT form,

$$
\text{bias}=\int e\,(\lambda-1)\,d\mathbb P_y ,
$$

and for the Hájek form (with $\bar\lambda=\int\lambda\,d\mathbb P_y$, $\bar e=\int e\,d\mathbb P_y$, up to an $O(1/n)$ ratio term),

$$
\boxed{\;\text{bias}=\frac1{\bar\lambda}\int(e-\bar e)(\lambda-\bar\lambda)\,d\mathbb P_y\;}
$$

The bias is a **product** of the map's error and the intensity's error. It vanishes if either is right:

- **The intensity is right up to a constant** ($\lambda$ constant): the map can be arbitrarily wrong.
- **The map's error is constant** ($e$ constant): the intensity can be arbitrarily wrong.
- **When both are a little wrong**, the bias is at most $\lVert e-\bar e\rVert\,\lVert\lambda-\bar\lambda\rVert/\bar\lambda$
  (Cauchy--Schwarz in $L^2(\mathbb P_y)$).

This is the *mixed-bias* property that defines double robustness [@rotnitzky2021]. In a design-based frame,
"the map is right" has a specific meaning: the map's error does not covary with where the floats go.

::: {.callout-note}
## Intuition
Floats crowd into cold water, so the mean field $\hat\mu$ runs cold where floats are sparse. The correction checks the
map against held-out floats, weighted so that every region counts by its area. It removes that offset as long as the
weights know where the floats crowd. They need to know it only where the map is wrong.
:::

**Variance.** Floats within a cohort are independent given the fold labels, so the correction is a sum of independent
float totals $u_j=\sum_{i\in j}v_ie_f(x_i)$. Its variance is estimated from those totals (delete-one-float jackknife within
cohort; for HT, $\sum_c\frac{n_c}{n_c-1}\sum_{j\in c}(u_j-\bar u_c)^2$). Correlation along a trajectory is absorbed into
$\operatorname{Var}u_j$, so no second-order intensity is needed. Like the survey estimators, this treats the map as fixed. The
variability of $\int\tilde Z_{-f}\,d\mathbb P_y$ across folds is not included, which is the known source of under-coverage.

## 6. Why the point rule leaves a bias floor

With point quadrature, the map term is $Q_y(\hat Z_{-f})$ instead of $\int\tilde Z_{-f}\,d\mathbb P_y$. Then

$$
\frac1F\sum_{f=1}^F\mathbb E\big[\hat\theta_f\mid\mathcal G_{-f}\big]-\theta_y
=\underbrace{\text{product bias}}_{\text{Section 5}}
+\underbrace{\tfrac1F\textstyle\sum_f\big[Q_y(\hat Z_{-f})-\int\hat Z_{-f}\,d\mathbb P_y\big]}_{\text{quadrature error of the maps}} ,
$$

where $\hat\theta_f$ is fold $f$'s estimate.

The correction $\hat C_f$ targets $\int(Z-\hat Z_{-f})\,d\mathbb P_y$, the error of the map *as a function*. It cannot see how the
map was integrated. Block kriging sets the second term to (numerically) zero, so only the product bias remains.

## 7. Comparison with survey sampling

| Survey difference estimator [@sarndal1992] | This report |
|---|---|
| Finite population $U$, total $\sum_U y_k$ | Continuum $\mathcal X_y$, integral $\int Z\,d\nu$ |
| Predictions $\hat y_k$ summed over all of $U$ | Map integrated over $\mathcal X_y$ (block kriging) |
| Inclusion probability $\pi_k$ | Intensity $q(x)$ (expected count per unit $\nu$) |
| $\sum_s(y_k-\hat y_k)/\pi_k$ | $\sum_i e_f(x_i)/q(x_i)$ |
| $\pi_k$ known from the design | $\hat q$ estimated by simulation |
| Fixed predictions (difference estimator) or fitted on the sample (GREG) | Cross-fit: fitted without the fold |
| Hájek / calibration to the known $N$ | Hájek / calibration to the known $\nu(\mathcal X_y)$ |
| Variance via $\pi_{kl}$, or with-replacement PSU form | Float totals as independent clusters |

The closest published form is @cicchitelli2012. They give the continuous-space version with a penalized-spline map
and a known inclusion density $\pi(x)$: $\frac1{|A|}\int_A\hat y\,dx+\frac1{|A|}\sum_j e(x_j)/\pi(x_j)$. That is our HT form without
cross-fitting and with $q$ known. Its variance uses the second-order inclusion density $\pi(x,x')$. Ours replaces that
with float totals, which is possible because floats, not profiles, are the independent units.

## 8. Comparison with AIPW in causal inference

For a mean outcome $\mathbb E\,Y$ with missingness $R\in\{0,1\}$ and propensity $\pi(X)=\Pr(R=1\mid X)$, the augmented IPW estimator
is [@robins1994; @bang2005]

$$
\hat\psi_{\mathrm{AIPW}}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\Big\{\hat m(X_i)+\frac{R_i\,(Y_i-\hat m(X_i))}{\hat\pi(X_i)}\Big\}.
$$

| AIPW | This report |
|---|---|
| Average of $\hat m(X_i)$ over a *sample* of units | Exact integral of $\tilde Z$ over the *known* measure $\mathbb P_y$ |
| $R_i/\pi(X_i)$: observed units reweighted | Points of $N$ weighted by $1/q$ (Campbell) |
| Propensity $\pi(X)$ | Intensity $q(x)$ |
| Propensity fitted to the same data | $\hat q$ from an independent simulator |
| Positivity $\pi\ge\epsilon$ | Coverage $\hat q\ge q_0$ and real floats reaching the domain |
| Cross-fitting [@chernozhukov2018] | Cross-fitting over floats |
| Normalized ("Hájek") AIPW | Hájek correction |
| Mixed-bias double robustness [@rotnitzky2021] | Same product form, in $L^2(\mathbb P_y)$ |
| i.i.d. units | Clustered point process; floats are the units |

The closest analogue is AIPW for **nonprobability samples** [@chen2020], where participation propensities are
estimated. Ours are estimated from a mechanistic model of how floats move, not from a regression on the sample.

Two features follow from the setting:

- **The "covariate distribution" is known exactly.** It is the domain measure, so the outcome-model term is an integral,
  not a sample average. That is why integrating the map well (block kriging) is part of the estimator, not a detail.
- **The intensity is identified externally.** A single realized float pattern cannot separate where floats tend to
  go from how they happen to clump. Many simulated realizations can.

## 9. Assumptions in one place

| Assumption | Used for |
|---|---|
| $\Lambda\ll\nu$, $q$ measurable and positive on $\mathcal X_y$ | HT identity (Campbell) |
| Folds of floats; floats independent within cohort given the labels | Conditional Campbell per fold; float-cluster variance |
| $\hat q$ independent of the evaluated data; $\hat q\ge q_0>0$ | Bounded weights; bias formula with $\lambda=q/\hat q$ |
| Same window and hyperparameters for all $x$ in a block | Block kriging equals the exact integral of $\tilde Z$ |
| Sub-grid fine enough for $\mathbf k_B$; $\int\tilde\mu\,d\mathbb P_y$ integrated exactly | Remaining numerical error negligible (checked by refinement) |
| Kernel $k$ and decomposition $\mu+a+\varepsilon$ | Efficiency only, not bias |
